docs.title: GameStart
docs.text:
Welcome! GameStart is a cozy first-person tidy-up game set in a late-90s/2000s video-game store. You're the overnight clerk: the whole shop starts out in a glorious mess, and box by box you put it back in order — game boxes on the right shelves, consoles on their stands, merch where merch belongs. No timers, no customers, no pressure. Just you, the hum of the CRT at the counter, and a store that slowly becomes yours.

The twist: if you choose to connect your Steam profile, the games on the shelves are your own library — your actual games appear as physical boxes you can pick up, flip over, and shelve. (Totally optional — there's a built-in fictional catalog too. See Privacy.)

Heads up: GameStart is in development and not yet released. This wiki describes the current development build. Anything marked Planned is design intent and may change before release.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Is the game out? Not yet — GameStart is in development. This wiki tracks the development build; pages mark in-development features as Planned.

What platforms? PC first (the game is built and tested for desktop). Anything beyond that is unannounced.

Do I need a Steam account to play? No. Connecting your Steam profile is optional — without it you get a full store of original fictional games. See Privacy.

Does my Steam data get uploaded anywhere? No. It's fetched from your public profile onto your machine and stays there. Privacy has the full breakdown.

Is there co-op? An early version is in the build. The title screen has an AFTER-HOURS CO-OP section: one player picks HOST CO-OP and shares the short CO-OP CODE, and a friend enters it and picks JOIN CO-OP. Treat it as a playground — the co-op store is separate from your solo night, nothing is kept when the session ends, and your solo save is never touched. Quiz fixtures stay solo-only in co-op for now. The full tidy-the-night-together co-op is still in design.

Is there a timer or fail state? No. No customers, no shifts to survive, no clock pressure — time of day is ambiance. The store only ever gets tidier.

Can I rebind controls? Yes, fully — keyboard/mouse and gamepad. See Getting Started for defaults.

I get motion sick in first-person games. A field-of-view slider is planned. Camera comfort options are a stated design goal.

Can I mod it? Yes — content packs can restock the store with custom fictional games, managed from an in-game screen. See Modding.

The last box — will I be hunting one lost item forever? The design explicitly guards against the "399 of 400" problem with tools already in the build: finished shelves keep a lit "done" gleam so what's left stands out, the Stock Sense glow outlines nearby copies of the game you're holding, and Tendril Grab reels loose strays of that game in from across your district — straight into your hands. See Talents & Gear.

Can I lose my save? The game never deletes a save. If yours is damaged or from a previous version, the title screen offers KEEP A COPY & START FRESH — the old save is backed up before a new night starts. See Getting Started.

docs.title: Controls (keyboard & mouse)
docs.text:
Every control can be rebound in the settings — this is the default layout.

Action Default Move W A S D Look Mouse Pick up / interact E or Left Click Put down / throw Right Click (hold to throw harder) Drop Q Cycle through what you're holding Scroll wheel, or tap R Inspect the held box (look closer) Hold V Open / close the game's case while inspecting Left Click (while holding V) Zoom in for a closer look Hold C Check the store map Hold Tab Use your gear (see Talents & Gear) G Cast a skill (see Talents & Gear) 1 2 3 4 5 6 Jump Space / B (tap or hold when charged jumping is enabled) Sprint (hold to run) Left Shift / L3 Crouch Left Ctrl Pause Esc

A thrown box goes where you are looking: aim up to lob it over something, aim at the floor to bounce it down in front of you. The longer you hold Right Click, the harder it flies — and the faster it spins flat like a frisbee on the way. A quick click still just tosses it gently at your feet, no spin.

While you hold a throw, the box in your hands starts to shake, and shakes faster the longer you hold — that rattle is your wind-up gauge, so you can judge the throw without looking away from where you're aiming. It settles the moment you let go, cancel, or pause.

Where charged jumping is enabled, tap for the shortest jump, release partway for a higher jump, or charge fully and release for the highest jump. If automatic jumping is enabled, reaching full charge jumps immediately. A green bar appears below the crosshair only while the jump is charging.

Gamepad is supported with equivalent bindings — except the skill keys 1–6, which are keyboard-only for now. While the Portal Pistol skill is waiting for you to aim (after pressing 6), Left Click places the portal and Right Click cancels — your usual pick-up and put-down come back as soon as the pistol is done or cancelled. Settings has a toggle-to-run option for Sprint, so you don't have to hold the key down.

docs.title: Your first night
docs.text:
Picking NEW GAME shows a STOCKING THE STORE loading screen while the night is set up — a counter ticks up as boxes are shelved (like 123 / 500 boxes shelved). The very first night can take a few minutes while cover art is prepared; later nights are much faster. When it finishes, you're in.

  1. Look around. The store opens in "arranged chaos" — games and merch piled on counters, fixtures, and the floor. Everything loose has a home somewhere.
  2. Pick things up (E / Left Click). You can carry a small stack at once — the counter in the corner of your screen shows how many you're carrying out of your max stack (like 3 / 8), and the list in the top-left shows everything in your pile, top to bottom — the first line is the item "in hand" (next to place). Scroll to flip through the stack and the list reorders with it. The pile you're carrying drifts with your gaze: look up and it settles low so you can see past it, look down and it rides up out of the way — you keep an edge of it in sight either way, and the list always tells you exactly what you're holding.
  3. Find the right spot. Hold a box near a shelf and a ghost preview shows where it would land. Once you've learned the Stock Sense skill, matching games glow to help you spot where the rest of the stack lives.
  4. Place it. If the spot is right, you get a satisfying chime and XP. If the box is in the wrong section, the shelf's price tag turns red — see Tidying & Price Tags.
  5. Check the terminal. The CRT computer at the counter is the store's brain: look up any game, see your play stats, and browse store info.

docs.title: Saving
docs.text:
The game autosaves when you pause. One store, one continuous save — progress you make stays made. When a save exists, the title screen shows CONTINUE; picking NEW GAME starts the night over.

If a save can't be continued, the title screen says why in plain words: it may be damaged, from a previous version of the game, from a newer version (update the game to continue), or it may need store content that isn't available any more — for example, after the store's stock lineup changed in an update. Whatever the reason, the fix is the same button: KEEP A COPY & START FRESH — your old save is backed up, never deleted, before the new night begins. If the title screen says it couldn't check your save right now, trying again is safe.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
The player's dictionary — every term here is something you can see or do in the game. (Developers/modders: the technical mapping lives in the Dev Glossary.)

Term Meaning After-Hours Co-op The title screen's early co-op mode — host a session, share the co-op code, and a friend joins your store. Separate from your solo night; nothing is kept when the session ends Bubble Carry Active skill (key 5) — seals your held box in a bubble that floats it to its home shelf on its own; if the shelf is full when it arrives, the bubble pops and the box settles nearby Portal Return Active skill (key 4) — set a return pad at your feet, link it to a shelf slot you aim at, and boxes you set down on the pad zip there Co-op code The short code a host shares so a friend can join their After-Hours Co-op session Deluxe Cart Passive skill — carry more boxes at once (two levels) Fictional catalog The store's built-in roster of original parody games, used when Steam isn't connected Gear The store gadgets your skills come from — see Talents & Gear Ghost preview The translucent outline showing where a held item would land Grand opening The finale: correctly shelf every physical copy and solve the required quiz, then flip the OPEN sign by the front door when you are ready. A NIGHT COMPLETE card sums up your shift — copies homed, titles complete, fixtures full, sections done, quiz shelves solved, talents learned, lifetime XP, and your time to grand opening — then the credits roll (skippable) Hall of Honor (Planned) Quiz fixture — rank your most-played games Plumbob Guide Passive skill — while you hold a box, a hovering gem marks the shelf where it belongs INFONET The store's information network — the counter terminal and Pip-Boy use it to show game details Inspect Holding V to bring the held box up close and read it Load order The #1, #2… order packs apply in — later packs win conflicts OPEN sign The sign by the front door. It reads CLOSED while the store still needs tidying; once the store is ready you can flip it to OPEN, which holds the grand opening and ends the night. In After-Hours Co-op only the host can flip it — the sign tells everyone else so — and when the host does, every player in the session gets the same grand opening Platform families The four game registers, each with its own box style: PayStation (blue), Newtondo (red), XRocks (green), and Vapor (black, the PC platform by Spout). Every family owns a grouped shelving district — PayStation west, Newtondo south, Vapor north-west, XRocks north-east — each continuing onto the mezzanine deck Pack A folder of custom content that restocks the store (Modding) Price tag The tag on a shelf rail under each run of games: white = right, red = something's in the wrong section Tendril Grab Active skill (key 2) — reels copies of the game you're holding in from across your district, shelf fronts and loose strays alike, straight into your hands; later levels reach the neighbouring districts, dig behind the front copy, and finally pull from anywhere in the store, the whole catch at once Section A themed area of the store (platform districts, free shelves, counter, merch) with its own overhead sign Mezzanine The store's upper deck, reached by two ramps — platform districts continue upstairs Section sign / plaque The overhead sign naming a section; (Planned) lights up when the section is fully tidied Shelf Guide Active skill (key 1) — lights up the spot where your held box belongs for a short time Store map The two-floor map of the store — hold Tab to raise your own paper copy; the same map hangs by the front door and stands on the directory Store directory The reading stand just inside the entrance carrying the store map You are here The red diamond on the store map marking your position; its notch points the way you're facing Hold Piece Signature skill that swaps the box in your hands with the front copy of a stocked shelf slot (not on the default Tool bar right now) Skills The pause-menu tab where talent points buy and upgrade skills; the active ones cast with keys 1–6 Staff-pick badge (Planned) The fuzzy "how much was this played?" hint on a box's back — deliberately never exact numbers Stock Sense Passive skill — while you hold a box, nearby copies of the same game get a purple outline Pip-Boy Active skill (key 3) — opens an INFONET readout for the box you're holding; press 3 or Esc to close it Portal Pistol Active skill (key 6) — Left Click opens an orange portal, another Left Click a blue one; step into either to walk out of the other at full speed. Right Click cancels while aiming Talent points The single upgrade currency, earned from quizzes and tidying, spent in the Skills tab Terminal The CRT computer at the counter — game lookup, play stats, store info Tidied / home An item sitting in its correct section, shelf, and row Wall of Shame The red challenge board — set five answers from least played up without giving up the copy in your hand, then press CHECK THE ORDER; ties share a rank

docs.title: Modding
docs.text:
GameStart's store stock is data-driven, and the game has built-in, player-visible modding surfaces: packs, content pack files (.gspack), and the title bank.

Pre-release note: the pack formats are still evolving. Packs you make today may need updates as the game develops.

docs.title: Packs
docs.text:
A pack is a folder of content that changes what fills the store: exclude games from the shelves, rename the fictional titles, or (in the classic browse mode) restrict which platform sections a game may stock.

In the game's pack screen you can:

  • See every installed pack (it says "No packs installed" until you add one).
  • Enable/disable each pack with its toggle.
  • See each pack's load order (#1, #2, …) — later packs win when two packs touch the same game.
  • Click "Open packs folder" to jump straight to where packs live on disk.

Packs now shape the night shift too: excluded games leave the pool the store stocks from, and fictional renames appear on box names. Excludes change which world a New Game builds — an existing save keeps the world it was made with, and its Continue will tell you if the pack set changed under it.

docs.title: Installing a pack
docs.text:
1. In the game, open the pack screen and click "Open packs folder".
  2. Drop the pack's folder in there (one folder per pack).
  3. Back in the game, enable it with its toggle.

docs.title: Content packs (.gspack)
docs.text:
A content pack is a single .gspack file that can carry deeper, gameplay- shaping data — today that means skills and talents (the gear you unlock and the talent trees behind it), with more content kinds on the same road. Packs are data only: no code ever runs from a pack, and every pack is strictly validated on load — a broken pack is skipped with a message, never a crash.

To install one: drop the .gspack file into the Mods folder next to your saves (%USERPROFILE%\AppData\LocalLow\<studio>\<game>\Mods). Rename it to <name>.gspack.disabled to switch it off. Load order is alphabetical; a pack made with gameplay content stamps itself into your save, so a save made with mods will refuse to continue if the mod set changes (protecting the save, not punishing you — restore the packs and it loads again).

docs.title: The title bank
docs.text:
The fictional titles on the boxes come from word banks you can replace: create Mods\titlebank.json with your own words —

{
  "sp3aNames": ["My Favorite Fake Game"],
  "adjectives": ["Copperleaf", "Mossy"],
  "nouns": ["Harbor", "Junction"]
}

— and the store names its stock from your banks on the next launch. Real trademarks are refused (the whole file is skipped if any word matches the deny list), and a malformed file just falls back to the built-in names.

docs.title: Steam Workshop
docs.text:
The first slice of Workshop support is in the game: subscribe to a GameStart Workshop item and the game installs it on the next launch — .gspack files land in Mods, folder packs land in the pack screen. Unsubscribe and it's removed the same way. (Publishing tools and the public Workshop hub go live with the Steam release — until then packs travel by file sharing, exactly as above.)

Planned next: sharable presets of your store settings, so you can hand a friend your whole store setup in one go.

docs.title: Making a pack
docs.text: The honest answer for now: the formats are documented for developers rather than polished for creators — a folder pack is a set of plain-text files, and a content pack is built with the in-editor Pack Workbench. If you're comfortable poking at files, see the Dev Glossary for where the technical documentation lives.

docs.title: What packs can't touch
docs.text: Packs can curate which games appear in the store, but they cannot switch the Steam connection on for you. That choice always remains yours — see Privacy. Packs also can't run code, load DLLs, or reach outside their own data — by design.

docs.title: Privacy — the optional Steam connection
docs.text:
Planned for Steam-enabled builds. The secure connection remains unavailable in the current pre-release until its Steam setup and on-Steam checks are complete.

When available, GameStart can put your own Steam library on the store's shelves. This page is the plain-English record of exactly what that means. The short version: it is opt-in and read-only. Limited library details pass through GameStart's online library service and may be held there for up to six hours.

The service runs on Cloudflare's network. Processing and temporary storage may happen in places where Cloudflare operates its service. Before this connection is made available, this page will name the country or countries used for temporary storage.

The connection starts off. You can enable it from the catalog screen; only your saved choice can turn it on. Installing or enabling a pack cannot connect Steam for you.

docs.title: What happens if you opt in
docs.text:
• The game asks the Steam app for a short-lived proof that you are signed in. It never asks for your Steam password.
  • GameStart's library service checks that proof with Steam, then requests your owned game titles, playtime totals, and last-played times. The service may temporarily keep your Steam account ID and your full owned-games list for no longer than six hours.
  • To prevent automated abuse, the service keeps a daily request counter for about 25 hours. That counter is not your connection address: it is a scrambled, one-way fingerprint of it, which cannot be turned back into an address.
  • The game downloads that limited list and fetches cover art onto your machine.
  • That data is used to fill the shelves, print the boxes, and generate the Wall of Shame challenge from your play history.
  • Cover art is cached locally so later sessions load faster.
  • Co-op is planned but not in the current build. When it arrives: if you host a session, the resulting shelf entries can be shown to the players who join you. Your sign-in proof and Steam password are never shared with them.

docs.title: What never happens
docs.text:
• Nothing from your library is bundled into the game — every player's store is prepared from the account that opted in.
  • The game cannot buy, sell, launch, or modify anything on your Steam account.
  • GameStart's publishing key is kept on the online service; it is not included in the game.

docs.title: If you opt out (or your profile is private)
docs.text: You get the fictional catalog — a full store of original parody games with authored stats. Everything works, including the Wall of Shame (it uses the fictional catalog instead of your backlog). You can change your mind either way at any time; the store restocks accordingly. Turning the connection off prevents new library requests. The service copy expires within six hours; locally cached cover art and the last downloaded list can remain until you clear the game's local data.

docs.title: Store Guide
docs.text: Your store is one big room with distinct sections. Learning the layout is the game — the better you know it, the faster every box finds its home.

docs.title: Finding your way
docs.text:
Three ways to get your bearings, all showing the same map:

  • Store map — hold Tab any time to raise a paper map of both floors. The red diamond is you; its notch points the way you're facing.
  • Store directory — the reading stand just inside the entrance, to your right as you walk in.
  • Wall map — mounted on the pier beside the front door.

The map colors match the marquee signs: each platform district fills in its band color, other sections in gray, the counter in red. Ramps are marked with arrows on both floor panels, and every color in the legend is paired with its printed name — you never have to rely on color alone.

docs.title: Sections
docs.text:
The store is now the two-floor layout: a big ground floor plus a mezzanine deck reached by two ramps — half the platform shelving lives upstairs.

  • Platform districts — every platform family owns a grouped district of wall bays: PayStation (blue) along the west, Newtondo (red) along the south, Vapor (black — the PC platform) in the north-west, and XRocks (green) in the north-east and east. Each district continues onto the mezzanine above it; the box shape gives every platform away (chunky cartridge boxes, slim jewel cases, tall keepcases, PC big boxes, little disc cases…). Colored marquee signs overhead mark each district.
  • Free shelves — the island gondolas in the middle of the floor (and a few on the deck): overflow space where any game box can live while you sort.
  • The counter — the heart of the store, under the north mezzanine strip: the register area and the terminal, a CRT computer where you can look up any game in the store and (if you connected Steam) your own play history.
  • Hardware & gear — the console-accessory wall on the east side stocks the console boxes (every platform and generation) alongside the peripherals; these keep their own homes off the game shelves.

docs.title: Reading a game box
docs.text:
The box itself tells you a lot:

  • Front: cover art, platform styling, title.
  • Back: publisher blurb, screenshots, and feature bullets — and, if you connected Steam, a shelf label with your logged hours and the year you last booted the game. Hold V to inspect a box up close; release V to lower it smoothly back into your hand.
  • Planned: the exact numbers move off the box into the terminal, replaced by a fuzzy staff-pick badge that only hints at playtime — never exact numbers.

docs.title: Section signs & plaques
docs.text: Each section has an overhead sign. Planned: when a section is completely tidied, its sign lights up and stays lit so the store itself becomes your progress bar. The store is ready for its grand opening once every physical copy is home and the required quiz is solved — and the front-door sign is what opens it. In After-Hours Co-op the sign belongs to the host: a guest's sign reads "Only the host can open the store." When the host flips it, everyone in the session sees the same grand opening.

docs.title: Genre dividers (dev-flag preview)
docs.text: With the shelf-composer dev flag enabled, the shelves show which genre they want in the style of record-store genre dividers: a colored rail runs along the shelf edge for the whole stretch that wants one genre, with a raised divider tab carrying the genre's name (ACTION, RPG, STRATEGY…) at the start of the stretch and a small matching tab closing its end. Neighboring slots on a shelf row that want the same genre share one divider group — each row of an Action bay on the PayStation wall reads as one named stretch, so every shelf row carries its own name tab along with its colored rail. Shelves open to anything wear a neutral gray divider tab reading Discount or Sale. Each genre keeps its own distinct color everywhere in the store, and the name is always printed on the tab, so you never have to rely on color alone. The dividers are guidance only: they never block items, and they only appear on boots where the composer's plan is active.

docs.title: Quiz walls
docs.text:
Special fixtures that quiz you on your own library:

  • Wall of Shame — the red challenge board: five answer slots under gold rank numbers, reading LEAST PLAYED → MORE PLAYED. Make a game active in your hand, aim at a slot, and interact to set that answer. A display copy appears on the board, but the real copy stays in your hand. Interact with an empty hand to clear an answer. Ties share a rank (a red bracket joins the tied slots). When you're confident, press the red CHECK THE ORDER plate. The five answers glow gold together when the order is right, or red together when it is wrong; changing an answer clears that result.
  • Hall of Honor (Planned) — your most-played games, ranked.

Getting the Wall of Shame right earns talent points (Talents & Gear) and is required before the grand opening. Price tags never appear on quiz fixtures — that would leak the answers. If you haven't connected Steam, the quiz uses the fictional catalog instead. Answer-setting quizzes are solo-only for now; co-op support is planned.

docs.title: Talents & Gear
docs.text: Talents are live end to end: earn talent points, spend them in the pause menu's Skills tab, and cast skills with keys 1–6.

docs.title: Talent points
docs.text:
One currency: talent points — money is gone from the store entirely. You earn them two ways:

  • Quizzes (the fast lane): complete the Wall of Shame correctly and get paid in talents. The Hall of Honor is planned.
  • Sorting (the slow trickle): regular tidying XP slowly converts into talent points on its own.

docs.title: The Skills tab
docs.text:
Open the pause menu and pick Skills to spend talents:

  • Your unspent talent points show at the top.
  • Available Active Skills appear first, in skill-bar order, followed by Passives. Active entries wear their current key badge; Passives have no key badge.
  • Levels get pricier as you climb: level 1 costs 3 talent points, level 2 5, level 3 7, and so on (two more each level). The Upgrade button always shows the exact price. Each entry shows your level (like Lv 2/10), the cooldown, and what every level improves; press Upgrade to buy the next one. A maxed skill says MAX.

docs.title: The skill bar (keys 1–6)
docs.text:
The skill bar always keeps six positions. Press keyboard keys 1–6 to cast. (The skill keys are keyboard-only for now — no gamepad binding yet.)

  • Unused positions say empty, unavailable skills say locked, and learned skills show their level.
  • A cast only "spends" the skill when it actually does something. If it can't work right now, a short hint pops up instead — like "Hold a box first", "On cooldown", or "No charges left" — and no cooldown starts.
  • Cooldowns refill on their own; higher levels mostly shorten them.

docs.title: Active skills
docs.text: Key Skill What it does 1 Shelf Guide Highlights the shelf where the box in your hands belongs — a beacon marks the spot for a short time; higher levels cut the cooldown 2 Tendril Grab Reels copies of the game you're holding in from across your district — shelf fronts and loose strays alike — straight into your hands, up to eight a cast. Level 2 reaches the districts next to you as well; level 3 digs behind the front copy; level 4 pulls from anywhere in the store and brings the whole catch in at once instead of one at a time 3 Pip-Boy Opens a large INFONET readout for the box you're holding. You can keep moving and handling boxes, but other skills wait; press 3 or Esc to close it. Dropping or throwing the scanned box also closes it 4 Portal Return Set a return pad at your feet, then aim at a shelf slot to link it — boxes you set down on the pad zip straight to that shelf 5 Bubble Carry Seals the box in your hands inside a bubble that floats it to its home shelf on its own — your hands stay free. If the shelf is full when it arrives, the bubble pops and the box settles nearby 6 Portal Pistol Arm it, then Left Click a wall or the floor to open the orange portal and Left Click again for the blue one — step into either and you walk out of the other, keeping your speed. Right Click cancels while you're aiming; the pair fades on its own after about half a minute

docs.title: Passive skills
docs.text:
Passives work all the time once learned — no key, no cooldown:

Skill What it does Deluxe Cart Carry more boxes at once — two levels, each raising your carry limit further Plumbob Guide While you hold a box, a hovering gem marks the shelf where it belongs Stock Sense While you hold a box, nearby copies of the same game get a purple outline — the "reunite the stack" glow

A note on the glow: highlighting matching games used to be free for everyone. It now belongs to Stock Sense — if you liked it, it's a cheap early buy.

docs.title: The retired gadget shelf
docs.text:
Gadgets were physical store gear — each a loving parody of infamous game-industry hardware. The classic shelf has since retired, its powers grown up and shipped as proper skills: the Sorter's Magnet's grab lives on in Tendril Grab, the Spotter Visor's scanner vision ships as the Pip-Boy skill and the Stock Sense glow, the Deluxe Pack ships as the Deluxe Cart passive, and the Pocket Terminal's database stays where it always lived — the counter terminal. The Buddy clocked out with the rest of the classic shelf. New gadgets may arrive with later store phases.

A note for quiz fans: quiz fixtures are designed to be solvable bare-handed — skills make them comfortable, never required.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text:
Pick up → find the right spot → place → watch the store come together. Every copy of a game has a proper home: the right section, the right shelf, the right row. When you hold a box near shelving, a ghost preview shows exactly where it would sit — and once you've learned the Stock Sense skill (Talents & Gear), other copies of the same game glow so you can reunite the stack.

Neaten a row anytime with Face (F) — pulling boxes forward into a tidy front line, just like real shelf work.

docs.title: Price tags: white good, red bad
docs.text:
Every row of games on a shelf has a price tag on the rail under it.

  • White tag — that run of boxes is where it belongs. All is well.
  • Red tag — something in that run is in the wrong section. Fix the placement and the tag turns white again, instantly.

If you place a box in a spot that fits but is the wrong section, the tag goes red on the spot — that's the store telling you "close, but no." No penalty, no timer; it just stays red until you make it right.

docs.title: One game, one home for the night
docs.text:
The first run where you correctly shelf a game becomes that game's chosen home for the night.

  • More copies placed in that run stay white.
  • Copies placed in another regular run show red, even when that section would normally suit the game.
  • The choice resets only after every copy of that game has been removed from regular shelves. The next correct placement chooses a new home.
  • Shelving skills use the chosen run too. If it cannot take another box, they wait instead of sending the box to a run that would show red.

docs.title: Finishing the night
docs.text:
Tidying makes the store ready; you decide when it opens. Once every physical copy is correctly shelved and the required Wall of Shame challenge has been solved, the store is ready and the OPEN/CLOSED sign by the front door comes to life. Your quiz answers do not consume the copies in your hand, so those copies still need their proper homes.

Nothing happens until you walk over and flip that sign to OPEN — so take as long as you like first, admiring the shelves or straightening one last stack. Flipping the sign holds the grand opening and ends the night.

Planned: when the last copy of a game is correctly shelved, that stack gets a persistent gleam — a little "done ✓" the store remembers. Finishing a section will also light its overhead sign.

docs.title: XP
docs.text: Correct placements earn XP (you'll see the +XP pop). XP raises your clerk level. There is no money in the store — your reward currency is talent points (Talents & Gear).
